maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
I just received this morning report No. 4 of the proceedings of the committee that was considering this bill. The committee scarcely considered the bill at all. There was a discussion between three or four members of the committee and the officials

Trans-Canada Air Lines
of the T.C.A. I cannot understand why the government is so anxious to rush this bill through the house. We had a debate on it the other day: but the second reading, as I contend, is the time to raise objections to a bill. The principle of the bill is one to which I have objected all these years. I am opposed to any monopoly in the air and to both the method and the manner of the civil aviation policy adopted by the present government. At the present time the Prime Minister is either in the old country or on his .way to Washington. We cannot say what effect the atomic bomb and the measures to which it may give rise will have on this whole question of civil aviation. I repeat what I contended at the time the resolution was first mentioned in- the house, namely, that it should be postponed until such time as the Prime Minister comes home.
As to the method of procedure, it will be noticed that when this matter was before the house, I believe on March 23 last, although it was required that the committee which had been set up on railways and shipping, should report back to the committee of supply when the committee reported back the words "committee of supply" had been struck out and it reported to the committee of the whole. The procedure, as I maintained at the time, is all wrong, it is when a bill is up for second reading that there should be a debate. At the conclusion of the debate on the resolution the minister rose and, although a motion requires forty-eight hours' notice, he moved that bill No. 21 be referred to the committee on railways and shipping, although the committee has nothing to do with civil aviation at all. How many meetings did that committee hold? Practically all its deliberations will be found in report of proceedings numbered 4. The committee met last Thursday, adjourned to meet again at four o'clock, and a discussion went on between only three or four members. It will be noticed that, although the committee on railway's and shipping consists of twenty-three members, the quorum was reduced from twelve to eight. When the bill or the resolution embodying its principles went before the committee it should have been understood that those who were interested in the matter -that is the existing aviation companies, the T.C.A., the Canadian Pacific Railway company, and the pioneer branch lines and others which have been pioneers in this field1-should be called before the committee and heard as to the merit.s of the bill, its financial provisions and all the rest of it. That procedure was not followed. The committee just met and whitewashed the whole bill. That is what it is- nothing but a whitewash. It will be noticed that a question was asked at that particular time by the hon. member for Rosedale, and a very proper question it was. He asked what properties the Canadian National Railways turned over to Trans-Canada Air Lines at North Bay. A small safe was mentioned, and the bill not examined at all. I fail to see that the committee complied with the text of the reference, namely to report on the bill itself.
What is to be the cost involved in these proposals? There is a legal matter involved of which the minister has probably not heard. I can tell him this, that the operators of any branch lines or pioneer lines can sue the government of Canada in the exchequer court for all the damages they incur. The principle was decided some years ago by the privy council in the Alberta Great Waterways case, in which the attorney-general of Alberta, the Great West Waterways and the attorney-general of Canada were involved. The privy council decided that when bonds were sold, securities marketed, vested rights of property pledged, and the like proceedings taken, a government is liable in respect of any interferences with private ownership and private rights as outlined and can be compensated.
This particular bill is linked up with what Canada did in Chicago and the agreement must be read into bill No. 21. We have all heard of the proposed agreements which the minister is now trying to get passed by the house and upon which debate was adjourned this afternoon. I will only say that, in adopting the method and manner which the government have proposed, they have abandoned any idea of an empire air scheme. The empire is entirely forgotten; we are simply linking ourselves up with Washington, and it is a leap in the dark. We do not know what will become of civil aviation in Canada. As I said in a debate on this subject eighteen months ago, reported in Hansard, March 31, 1944, at page 2046:	-
We know what science properly applied has done in the last seventy-five years in the utilization of oil, gas and falling water and many other agents of power and industry. It has won the admiration of the whole civilized world. Why? Because science argues from fact; it does not argue in the realm of doubt and opinion. Look at the progress which medicine has made in the last fifty years.
I went on to refer to the fact that the minister's policy of establishing a monopoly in connection with civil aviation in Canada would lead to these factors being ignored, and said:
Canada should try to take the lead in the field of design and should prepare a definite policy for the next twenty-five years. Aviation in Canada is yet only in its infancy. Research,

Trans-Canada Air Lines

design and experimentation will be more important than ever. In Canada and in the empire we are on the threshold of a grand new age which will revolutionize aeroplane construction and the development of aeroplane engines. In this field high speed is essential to supremacy. Problems of all sorts arise; science and research will provide even lighter alloys and new types of wings,_ engines and parts which will withstand various climatic conditions the world over.
I went on to say:
We are now embarking upon a policy of complete isolation from the mother country; we are going over the heads of Australia and New Zealand, and I say we are at the parting of the ways. I warn hon. members of the danger; I say we should stop, look and listen to the advice of those who have seriously considered this matter. When the young people come back fimn the war and look for employment where will they find it? The other night reference was made to Russia. That country will have nothing to do with this internationalization of air routes; neither will the United States.
I have no papers now with me to-day. I had no knowledge that this matter was coming up. But I wish to refer to one or two matters which relate to what may be called the preamble of the bill, because this is probably the last chance w,e shall have.
I cannot understand why more hon. members of the opposition have not risen to oppose a second reading of the bill, because I can truthfully say that I never believed we should be called upon to pass a measure of this kind. How does it come about that a minister of the crown can go to a conference at Chicago and approve four different sets of agreements over the head of parliament which are practically comprised in bill No. 21, with the Chicago agreements read into it, that we are to be asked to pass? A minister of the crown goes to Chicago to attend a conference at the invitation of the United States, and what, does he do? He commits this country to a certain course of action in connection with aviation that will cost millions. I contend that no minister should be allowed, over the head of parliament and while this house is in session, to go to Chicago or anywhere else and make an agreement that is binding upon this country. A constitutional change should veto that. We did this sort of thing in connection with the Kellogg and Locarno pacts and again in connection with the covenant of the league of nations, and when the Abyssinia affair was at its crisis we passed sanctions against Italy. Then another minister rose in his place and abandoned what had already been done by the Prime Minister and vetoed the sanctions. There should be a constitutional change that would make it impossible for any minister of the crown to enter into any such agreements that bind the Canadian people in this way.
Who is to pay the costs entailed by this agreement? Who paid for the war anyway?

Not the ministers. They paid something toward the total, but it is the Canadian people in all the constituencies represented in this house; it is the taxpayers, who paid for the war, and they are the people who will pay again if we pass a bill like this and bankrupt the country. And we are passing this bill with the Prime Minister away.
The conference at Chicago was not attended by Russia. Great Britain was there; she would not have anything to do with it, and has not yet signed it. Britain had already made an agreement with Russia for ten years, and so the United States remains the author of the policy laid down at Chicago. The United States have also entered into secret agreements with a large number of the Latin republics, and this without any regard to the mother country or Russia or the dominions.
The minister has not considered, in connection with this bill, the possible effects which the atomic bomb will have on civil aviation. Apparently that question has not entered his mind, and at this moment the Prime Minister is on his way to Washington to discuss the question. I wonder if the minister has looked into the report submitted by the Kilgore subcommittee of the United States senate that has been considering the question of civil aviation in its post-war development. It is a valuable report on the effect of the allied bombing of Germany. That committee in its report made a reference to the prediction of H. G. Wells and other enthusiasts, before the great war started, that the aeroplane would destroy the enemy in a short time, and when the war was all over, as the committee points out, Germany had a tremendous equipment in machine tools, iron and steel, and the possibility of producing synthetic rubber on a large scale.
When the minister was at Chicago he apparently forgot the contribution which Canada made to the great empire training scheme.
I fail to see that T.C.A. has benefited by or considered at all in its set-up the work done by the training of thousands of young men during the war, in our war air scheme, one of the glories of the late war. Everyone thought that aviation would provide a great source of employment for these brave young R.C.A.F. men, so many of whom died in the battle of Britain.
I referred a moment ago to the Kilgore subcommittee of the United. States senate. That committee published a valuable report on the results of the allied bombing of Germany, and its findings are relevant to the bill before us. The committee states:
When it was over Germany still had four million tons of machine tools capable of immense armament output, the iron and steel industry

Trans-Canada Air Lines
with minor repairs was capable of producing twenty-five million tons yearly, the dye and chemical industry which produces explosives was virtually untouched as also the synthetic rubber plant.
The general damage done to German war output was only twenty per cent.
Bill No. 21 fails to consider this union of civil and war aviation.
I doubt if lion, members now in the house have read the report presented by the committee on railways and shipping with reference to bill No. 21. I read it only this morning when I got it, and I do not believe that five members in this house have read it. If they have, then I am shocked to find that the merits of the bill are not being discussed in the committee. We had a cross-examination * of Mr. Symington. That is all very well; as a private citizen Mr. Symington is all right. But in my opinion he was one of those who contributed to the mistakes made in connection with the Canadian National Railways in this countiy. The Royal Canadian Air Force has received very little aid or recognition from the operations of T.C.A. They prefer America first. When the pilots got out of the war they received little encouragement from Trans-Canada Air Lines; few were drafted by the T.C.A., and if we pass this bill they will get less encouragement in the future. It is the duty of the opposition to examine the bill. If the war had lasted another twelve months I do not think we would have heard anything about this bill, because science would have developed a much greater number and variety of atomic bombs.
I do not believe that science deliberately set out to split the atom in order to discover some terribly destructive weapon, nor do I believe that the late Lord Rutherford ever contemplated its development for war purposes; and if we pass this bill we shall simply be ignoring the questions that will be discussed at the atomic conference which is shortly to take place in Washington. In view of what I have said, Mr. Chairman, I think the committee should rise and report progress and ask leave to sit again, because we have had no opportunity to read the report of the committee on railways and shipping.
The United States and Britain were in the war together fighting a common enemy, and during that time Britain was unable to look after the cause of civil aviation in the Pacific as she would otherwise have done. The result is that the United States has captured the whole Pacific territory. When they were here both Mr. Curtin and Mr. Fraser made strong appeals to Canada for cooperation in the development of aviation in the Pacific, and for an empire air scheme, as they did 47696-1191
in January, 1944, but those appeals have been ignored by the government in this bill. The mother country has been left out altogether, and there is no hope of an empire air scheme. As I have said, the government has failed to consider the agreement between Britain and Russia and the various agreements that the United States has entered into with South American countries. I protest against this bill for the various reasons that I have given all last year and this year. I do not believe that it is in the public interest.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
This bill changes the whole set-up as regards civil aviation in Canada, and possibly it is well to review the whole question of the Canadian aviation policy. Active aviation in Canada is from thirty to forty years old. During the first world war it assumed sizable proportions and in 1925 became commercially important in the development of bush operations-and everyone knows what bush operations have meant to the country.
Canadians have taken to the air as the people of the British Isles did to the sea but I believe that, given an opportunity for . development, there is no reason why we in Canada cannot be leaders m the air as our forbears in Britain were in world shipping.
There are many fields in transportation in which the surface carrier is and probably will always remain much more efficient and more useful than the aeroplane. The planning of aviation policy requires a full knowledge of the capabilities of all forms of transport and an understanding of those fields in which the aeroplane is superior and will, therefore, eventually take the business. These include many entirely new types of transportation. The planning of an aviation policy must, therefore, be based on the fundamental fact that air transport does not eliminate the older forms, but is complementary to, and additional to them, and by wise and farsighted planning can be-used to increase the rate of development of the countiy in fields which could not formerly be reached.
In most parts of the world, the tendency has been to develop air services parallel to existing lines of communication, and for many of the older countries this was the only form of air transport development which took place. This type of flying is essential in a progressive world for the fast movement of passengers and mail and some varieties of express. At the same time, it is foolish to wink at the fact that it is not, and probably will never be, a replacement for the older methods of transport. The man whose time means money travels by air because he saves time and, consequently, expense. He used to take a drawing-
Trans-Canada Air Lines

room on the train. The passenger, however, who travels in a day-coach will for a long time to come continue to travel in that way. It must, however, be borne in mind that, even though the cost of air transportation has been considerably reduced in recent years, it is by no means as cheap as transportation, by rail, and rail costs are also coming down. The same applies in an even greater degree to most classes of freight. The result has been that, excluding the war years which are not representative of normal business conditions, intercity air line operations have normally required subsidization running up to as much as fifty per cent or more of the total revenue of the company.
In Canada we have an opportunity for the development of profitable air operations such as is available in few other countries in the world; this is the bush transportation field. In these regions, the alternative methods of transportation are frequently very expensive. They are in general not only slow but are restricted by seasonal climatic conditions, and the relatively small volume generally makes them very expensive per unit carried, as well as making the cost of the ground facilities such as roads, docks, portage railways and stopping places excessively high when calculated on the same basis.
The aeroplane on the' other hand thrives under these conditions. Immediate service can be given without the necessity of building extensive ground facilities, and the service is so flexible that it can be built up to any desired scale immediately the demand is found to exist. It is not restricted by change of season and, in the more remote parts of the country particularly, is not confined by the type of terrain. Even on a straight basis of cost the operational advantages for many types of work are so greatly in favour of the aircraft that it actually becomes cheaper pound for pound than other available forms of transportation.
It is unfortunate that the histoiy of civil aviation in Canada contains so little evidence of sound planning and aggressive government action to foster the development of bush operation. It is quite true that after long delay a determined effort was made to provide a first-class inter-city air sendee and, while the facilities now available on Trans-Canada Air Lines, and the quality of operation which is maintained, are exceedingly good, they are by no means the equal of those available on the main lines in the United States. They are, however, maintained at considerable expense to the public, and the sole operating agency, Trans-Canada Air Lines, receives public support in the form of payment for mail, a direct

cash subsidy, and provision of landing facilities and navigational aid on a scale which is by no means intensively utilized by the limited amount of air traffic from this single line.
The bush services on the other hand-although for nearly twenty years they have filled a vital economic place in the country's development, have done more than any other agency to speed the opening up of the north country, and have given employment both directly and indirectly to far more people than has the government-owned air line-have received no such assistance.
Mail contracts which are used in practically all countries of the world as a means of assuring transportation companies a basic revenue, have in the case of bush operations, been handled in a most parsimonious manner. The contracts were usually written to include a thirty-day cancellation clause. In many cases no contract at all was signed, so that the company was denied even this limited protection. Specifications commonly required a straight poundage rate for which the carrier was obliged to guarantee a fixed schedule of deliveries without any assurance of the volume of mail which he would receive. Competitive bidding was carried to such an extent that mail, although taking more space than normal express, was actually carried at rates below the prevailing express rates, and in one case at least the carrier was required to transport all outbound mail free of charge. Most other government business was offered for open competitive bidding in order to secure the cheapest possible price, and it was not an unheard of practice on occasion for the quotation of one company to be made known to a rival firm in order to secure a lower bid. During all this time there has been no attempt on the part of the civil government agencies responsible for commercial aviation to provide any of the ground facilities or navigational aids in bush areas which are considered as a normal public expense in the assistance of the transcontinental service.

speechtext:
I am only referring to my notes. It is true that in the middle of nineteeni-thirties the so-called transport act on aviation as regards bush pilots was introduced. The objective set forth was to assure uniformity of standards of operation, safety for the public and all those things that were considered requisite at that time for people in the flying industry. The act was strongly protested against by almost eveiy company. Among the reasons they gave was one that it placed great-restrictions on their operations. The result was that in the main the companies were made to operate on a basis on which they could not and did not make any money.
We are now coming to the post-war era. We have a tremendous number of young men who have been in the air force, experienced men and many others who have acquired a liking for outdoor life, and who should be the pioneers to open up the north country. All that is offered to them is a traffic survey to be conducted by men who have little if any experience in the bush transport business. At this time I should like to say that it is my opinion that aviation in Canada should be placed under one minister. It should not be handled ii#a department where the minister has many other duties and is busy the whole time. I am of opinion that as far as Canada is concerned all aviation should be placed, in the hands of one minister, with two deputies, one handling civil aviation and the other, military aviation. I believe much of the training carried on by the Royal Canadian Air Force is largely applicable to commercial work. I have in mind particularly photography, surveying and other services of which we can make use in our great north land. The men serving in the Royal Canadian Air Force under this set-up would get a great deal of excellent training in navigation, photography and in many other branches.
Under this bill we are going to put out of business a competitor of Trans-Canada Air Lines. The balance sheet of Trans-Canada Air Lines, which was produced in this house some time ago, showed a very small margin of profit on its operations for the last fiscal year; but it was pointed out that the president of the company received no salary. Had he
received a salary the company would have been in the red; and had the Department of Transport charged Trans-Canada Air Lines for all the sendees that have been made available by that department I feel sure the deficit would have been even greater.
We in this house are interested in seeing that civil aviation in this country is placed on a sound footing. Many times a, majority of the people of Canada have expressed their disapproval of the amalgamation of the two railways, which would have resulted in a state monopoly. For the same reason I believe the people of this country will disapprove the desire of the minister to have Trans-Canada Air Lines the only worth-while air transportation company in Canada. I suggest to the minister that before he does away with the competitors of Trans-Canada he give consideration to what will be the result of such action. My own opinion is that I can see no reason why Canadian Pacific Air Lines as such should not be allowed to compete with Trans-Canada in both the transcontinental and trans-oceanic runs. In the first place, I would rather see Canadian Pacific Air Lines in this business than the Dominion of Canada, because I am positive that transoceanic air routes will not be a paying proposition. Answering a question in committee the other day, Mr. Symington was asked in regard to the proposed routes, and on page 191 of those proceedings he replied:
We have given a great deal of study to these routes. I might state quite frankly to this committee that I believe they will be losers for some time to come and require financial aid. We would prefer to run to Australia and New Zealand via Fairbanks, China, India and Australia, or I should say China-Australia. But that is not now open because of Russia. Therefore we expect to land at Hawaii and on down to Australia and New Zealand under a joint agreement with Australia and New Zealand. That operation depends upon when you get the equipment with which to run it. Because they are long hops you have got to be sure that you have the proper equipment. What the financial result will be I cannot prophesy at all. It depends upon how many people are going to travel and how much mail is carried-
Then this is the important part, because this is the opinion of the president of Trans-Canada Air Lines:.

but I would not rvant to invest my money in it, if I had any to invest.
That is what the president of Trans-Canada Air Lines thinks of the trans-oceanic routes, in connection with which we are being asked now to increase the capital of Trans-Canada Air Lines. When the president of the company has such a doleful outlook on thtse

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, possibly I can help to expedite matters by confining my remarks to the section before -the committee. By this section it is proposed- to increase the capital from $5,000,000 to $25,000,000. This amendment offers tremendous possibilities, because, it seems to me it places in the hands of the minister a great deal of authority which I doubt it is wise to do. I do not say that in any disrespectful way of the present minister. I think it is thoroughly understood that I have a fine appreciation of -the minister presenting this bill. His long years of public life indicate the confidence that is placed in him.
However, we are dealing with the granting of authority which will be delegated to his successors. We may have sufficient confidence

Trans-Canada Air Lines
in the minister to place this authority in his hands, but it may lead to something which we do not at this time anticipate. I find it difficult to speak on a measure Q.f this kind and not be misunderstood, because it clashes somewhat with one's ideas of public and private ownership. I am presenting my % observations only from the point of view of monopoly, whether it be a public or private monopoly. I feel it would be unwise for Canada to contemplate a monopoly in air transportation under public ownership. _
This country offers tremendous possibilities for air development. As a matter of fact, I think the future of Canada, with its vast expanse of territory, is a challenge to our imagination and our determination to bring into effect transportation which will knit this country more closely together. I am assuming certain things, because the matters I intend to refer to are not written in the bill. Because of remarks which have been made in this house on former occasions it would appear that the object is to have one central authority. That object, as I interpret the bill, is to bring air transportation entirely under one authority, whereas my own considered opinion is that this country could well afford to encourage others to engage in air transportation. It might not be feasible to have various companies engaging in these activities if their resources were not sufficient to carry them through, but I do believe that we might well anticipate our country being opened up and developed by two great air transportation systems run in connection with our two railway systems, each one developing its own individual lines and bringing about an element of competition which, in my opinion, would lead to more efficient .service.
I have also in mind the young men who have served this country during the war years in the air service and who might want to make a career in air transportation. I consider that it is important from that point of view that we should have more than one air transportation system in this country.
I am reminded also of the international aspect. It seems to me that if our goverm-meat operates our air lines, there is bound to be competition and1 interlocking with the services of our great neighbour to the south and perhaps with other countries, so that the government might become sometimes the victim of its oWn system, involving this country in a dispute through some infringement of the laws of another country. There would not be that danger with a private company.
The present stage of development of our Trans-Canada Air Lines is a credit to whoever claims the responsibility for it, but the
possibilities before us are so great that I think we should contemplate having a full-time minister for air transport in Canada. Canada could well afford to give leadership' in this field. We have tremendous possibilities compared with those of many other nations. When I think of what the smaller European nations like Britain and the Scandinavian countries have achieved1 in the shipping world I wonder if we are not taking too much for granted in assuming that Canada will not rapidly develop through air transport and other modern means of communication.
I should like to know more about the objects of this bill. I should like to be certain just what it seeks to accomplish. Is there no danger of setting up a public monopoly? Is it the intention to expand our air transportation and at the same time offer an opportunity to those who care to engage in air transport whether they have limited capital or unlimited capital? That is what I am chiefly concerned about, not with the bill itself particularly, because capital will no doubt be needed if the system is to expand. But I think that we should have an assurance from the minister as to the real objects of the bill. Does it contemplate monopolizing air transportation, or are we to give private enterprise an opportunity to share in the development- of this newer means of transportation?

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
It is usual, in speaking in this house, to say immediately that you "had not intended to take part in this debate." The only reason I am rather different from, anyone else is that I really mean it. I have only two thoughts to express which are, perhaps, a question.
In the first place, I wish the minister would tell us something about the route from Fairbanks to Whitehorse. Unfortunately I have been away recently, through no fault of my own, neither was it any good fortune of my own. But I know that Canadian Pacific Air Lines were anxious to carry out that route, which is, I believe, approximately only four hundred miles. They were quite prepared to do that with no expense other than gasoline.
I noticed in my reading on the train a day or so ago that the minister said that Trans-Canada Air Lines was taking that as an international route and had leased to Canadian Pacific Air Lines that area; I think I am quoting fairly correctly. Then I remember reading about two men from the Edmonton chamber of commerce who came here, one of them a great friend of mine of the name of G. Becker, an old pilot and1 a man of much experience not only in flying but in the direction of the industry of flying. He is a grand person, and one of his greatest recommendations was that he was an excellent Liberal, and therefore would do vers7 well for the Edmonton chamber of commerce in get- '. ting that line opened. The simple fact is that some time ago, when most of those people wanted to go from Fairbanks to the eastern borders of the United States, C.P.A. was not

Trans-Canada Air Lines
allowed to fly from White Horse to Fairbanks and back, but it could have been done without any change of schedule, and T.C.A.,
I think, would have received the major portion of that money, which would have meant more United States dollars in Canada, which,
I am sure, the Minister of Finance would assure us was a desirable object. That was never done, but the answer now is that it is being done and that C.P.A. has been chosen to do it.
On the general principle involved' in this bill, I would say that I agree with, the idealistic idea. I remember, a certain prime minister of this country, now a lord overseas, saying to me that private people had taken the water and the land, but "By Jove"-I think that was his roughest expression-"the country would retain the air"-I think that is the way he put it and he is that man who started this business.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
I am now
coming to the "hear hear" boys over on my left.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: That's the stuff.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: Their attitude is this, that "the country"-and by that, of course, they mean the government-should own and operate everything, the means of production, the sources of production. I arp now one of those people -I am not suggesting that I am speaking for my party at all, but I want to make it plain, and I hope I can be heard from here to Calgary-who are utterly opposed to government ownership and operation of anything. Let us make that plain. A great example of government ownership, according to our hon. friends on my left, is the post office; it is a "natural" to use an expression of my learned and1 hon. friend. I beg the hon. member's pardon, but I have been engaged so long in law. May I just say that I apologize to my hon. friend for saying he was learned. I did not mean that.

Let us take some other examples of this government ownership we are talking about, and to which the minister-I think his most
recent title is Minister of Reconstruction-has become such a convert. I will admit that he had a Moses in the old days who lived rather close to the place where I lived. As I say, the post office is cited to us as a grand example of government ownership and operation.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT

There is your first example of government ownership.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT

Let us now talk about liquor. Some people do not like to talk about liquor, but I am anxious to.
I am one who, on the odd occasion, when I have a friend who will give me a little, will try it, but I will not admit I go any farther than that. In eight provinces of Canada what happened? Under government ownership and operation, for it was nothing else, they not only increased the price-they never heard of the price ceiling-but they adulterated the product. The question of public ownership versus private ownership bobs up frequently in this debate. I think I may say that I am neither for public ownership per se nor for private ownership per se. It is a question of whether or not one kind of ownership can give better service and better opportunities to our Canadian people.	.
I take my stand on this present matter on the side of private ownership, because I believe that in a new and developing and fast-growing industry, such as the air transport industry promises to be and to become, the people of Canada will be better served if that industry is left, if not entirely in the hands of private enterprise, at least so that private enterprise will have an opportunity and at the same time there will be opportunity for our boys.
We as a country, and the world, are just' on the threshold of air transportation. I shall perhaps give some figures later to indicate why that is so.
Young men in Canada to-day, unless they wish to join a government service, or what is virtually a government service, because the T.C.A. is wholly government owned, cannot get into this air transport industry. Despite the assertions of Mr. Symington in committee that he is the boss, I think we in this chamber know pretty well who is the boss of T.C.A. One need only trace the history of that corporation through the various ministries that we have had since its inception to know that it has continued under one minister, and that he is the boss of T.C.A. Therefore it happens that young men who want to go into this great air transport industry cannot do so unless they wish to become virtually civil servants, with all the restrictions which such an occupation puts upon one, not only restrictions as to opportunity, but certain difficulties in regard to political opinions, and so forth; or perhaps one is forced to have no political opinion whatsoever as a citizen of this country. The result is that young men-and already the trend has been in operation

must go to another country. That trend, of course, is across the border. We find that many young graduates in engineering and science go across the border anyway, but when one puts an artificial restriction on their opportunity, such as a government monopoly of this small, but soon to grow into a vast service, we find that these young men must go

to another country after the expense of bringing them up and educating them has been borne by our own country.
I could not help feeling a real sense of sorrow when I attended a class reunion just two Saturdays ago to find how many letters from graduates were from boys and even girls who are now in the United States. It seems that Canada, coming through two wars as it has, has lost many of the cream of its manhood in the sacrifice to preserve our liberty and) our nationhood; and then, on top of that, we have lost so many to our neighbour across the way which can present such vast opportunities. On top of that, we find that the government of the day encourages that attitude by taking unto itself the sole proprietorship of a substantial part of air transportation. That makes one wonder just what opportunities there will be in the way of attractions to our young men and women as compared with attractions across the border.
We do not find in this bill what will happen to the present air transportation lines in this country which will have to be divested by Canadian Pacific Air Lines because of its association with the Canadian Pacific Railway company. I do not think the government has given any serious thought to what will happen to any of those lines, and there are several references in this regard in the evidence of the committee. I inquired whether or not any of this 825,000,000, of which $20,000,000 is new capital about to be authorized, would be used in acquiring any domestic companies in Canada, and I was told by the minister:
We will not acquire any domestic company in Canada under this act.

matter of T.C.A. policy or as a matter of government policy?
We now come to the matter of who runs these TranS-Canada Air Lines and just how close they are to the government. The minister then replied:
I state it as both; I am stating it to be government policy.
May I point out to the committee that the men who are operating Canadian Pacific Air Lines are men who, for the most part, were veterans of the last war. We in this committee to a man are, I believe, solicitous of what is to happen to the veterans of this war. We have a veterans committee which is so much concerned about the matter that it sits no less than five days a week in order to make sure that justice is done to the veterans of this war. Then he became a notable bush pilot, and later helped in the development of Canadian Pacific Air Lines. When a country engages in foreign transport it immediately runs into possibilities of international difficulties. While I do not wish to labour this point, nevertheless I think it should be brought before the committee. While it is true that the T.C.A. will be a separate legal entity,' if the line should get into difficulty in a foreign country, say Brazil, it is not beyond the bounds of possibility that this country might be involved with that foreign country. If the foreign operated line were owned by private capital, there would be no likelihood of that occurring. There have been such cases, I understand, in South America. where presidents occasionally flee the country, sometimes taking part of the national treasury with them. If they go on a foreign boat, the country with which it is registered may become subject to possible popular outcry and be involved in diplomatic difficulties.
This committee cannot give too serious attention to the future of air development. If present signs are any indication, it will be one of the great fields of transportation. I

should like to read a report of a forecast made by the civil aeronautics division of the United States government, as follows:
"Civil aviation, more than any other existing industry," the survey states, "offers the immediate hope of creating many new sources of livelihood, not only directly, but through allied and grass-routes sources."

We have an industry which is currently putting in the United States treasury a profit of more than $50,000,000 a year through the excess of air mail revenues over payments of carriers.
The subject now before the committee is one of vast import and the committee cannot give too great consideration to it. Because of its largeness and the great potentialities which it presents, it is my firm belief that more opportunities and greater service will be afforded to the Canadian people if private enterprise is allowed to compete with government ownership in this great and expanding field.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
I am not going to enter into this controversy regarding public ownership or private ownership. As a matter of fact, the person who enjoys most that particular controversy is the minister, because it enables him to take a rest while it continues.
I have a couple of questions I should like to ask the minister in order to bring him back into the discussion. The first is this: If the capital is increased as is contemplated by this bill, will any portion of that increase be used in connection with the operation of lines within Canada? I see that under sections 20 to 25 inclusive provision is made- and it is somewhat of a novelty, I think-for the setting up of other corporations by Trans-Canada Air Lines. I am going to refer to the sections in question, so that the minister will be able to give an answer to this question, which apparently was not answered or was not asked during the committee's sittings. Section 20 states that "The governor in council may on the petition of the corporation declare that a'ny number of persons named in the petition . . . shall be a body corporate", and then it goes on to set out the circumstances connected with these companies so set up. Then there is this amazing provision, that "the governor in council may authorize the minister to enter into a contract with any corporation incorporated" under these provisions "for the organization, operation and maintenance of air services designated from time to time by the governor in council". Therefore I ask the minister if any portion of this S20 million increase to be used for the setting up of these other corporations which the governor in council will be empowered to set up to provide for corporations which are to confine their operations within the dominion.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: And that no portion of the $20 million can at any time be turned over to corporations set up by the governor in council to operate within Canada?

speechtext: Where is there anything in the statute that bears out that categorical promise on the part of the minister? A further question comes to mind. As I understand the situation, unless that suggestion is adopted this measure can be used as a backdoor method to take over these air lines by the setting up of these corporations. The power is there; once parliament gives this power it can be utilized; whatever private air lines these corporations set up by the governor in council desire to take over they can take over. Trans-Canada Air Lines

The second thing I wish to bring to his attention is this: has there ever been in this country a case where a government has asked for the power of the governor in council to set up corporations in the manner provided for in sections 20 to 25? I do not know of any. .

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
I am not speaking about mail contracts. That brings me to this question of the M. & C. Aviation company of Prince Albert. On April 7 of this year an order in council was passed, making provision for the payment of a subsidy to the M. & C. Aviation company. This company operates in Prince Albert and was operating there before the war. During the war period it enj oyed a very large business in connection with war production, and I note that the order in council states that, upon the recommendation of the air transport board, it is in the opinion of the undersigned desirable, pending full examination and consideration of the possible relations to the post-war air services of the operations of the company, to maintain the company's present operations, and to subsidize the company in amounts not exceeding a total of $12,000 for a period of one year commencing April 1, 1945. This order in council was passed under the Aeronautics Act, the War Appropriation Act and the War Measures Act. This company was not concerned in the operation of these air lines. There was nothing connected with the military affairs of the country.
I should like to know why, in the setting up of this subsidy scheme, it was passed under the AVar Appropriation Act and the War Measures Act. What were the circumstances

under which this subsidy was provided for? In addition to the subsidy, this company has mail contracts and receives regular fees or, indirectly, subsidies, as the minister suggests, under these contracts. On whose recommendation was the subsidy paid to the company, and is it indicative of a change of viewpoint on the part of the government that certain companies, or all private companies, operating feeder services shall be considered as having an opportunity available to them from time to time of receiving subsidies?
That is a very dangerous situation. I see there is a provision, under section 25 of the new bill, which says that "the governor in council may authorize the minister to enter into a contract with any corporation incorporated under section 20 of this act, for the organization, operation and maintenance of air services designated from time to time by the governor in council." It is also provided that they may provide for terms of payment of subsidy to the corporation.
I ask the minister this question: Is he not thereby given a power which might very well be abused, which will allow the minister to designate such companies as he feels are entitled to it to receive subsidies, thereby being placed in unfair competition with other companies operating under similar conditions and [DOT] similar circumstances? What actually will take place under that section if carried to its logical limit is that, without limitation, parliament will in advance be granting to the minister or the governor in council power to make unlimited expenditures, because no limitation is placed on these expenditures under the section for subsidies.
That is a very dangerous and comprehensive power for parliament to place in the hands of a minister or the governor in council. I suggest to the minister that, so far as section 25, subsection 1 is concerned there should be added thereto words of limitation providing that the- organization, operation and maintenance of the air services designated from time, to time by the governor in council shall be beyond the territorial limits of Canada.
Provision should also be made in this bill to limit the amount of subsidy, or the power of the minister and' the governor in council, if any power is granted, instead of giving carte blanche. AVhat we are actually doing under this section is granting in advance to the governor in council uncontrolled, undefined powers of granting subsidies to such companies as are set up, thereby indirectly securing appropriations in advance without the authority of parliament. I suggest that the minister, in regard to those sections, should give consideration to an amendment in order to limit

Trans-Canada Air Lines
the power, because we are witnessing session after session the granting by parliament to the executive, the governor in council, and the minister, extraordinary powers without control on the part of parliament, and' that is a trend) that must be put a'stop to.
Reading the debates in the British House of Commons, one thing that impresses me was the fact that, as soon as the war was over, every endeavour was made by the Churchill government, and now by the Labour government, to ensure that extraordinary powers such as are within the provisions of these sections shall be strictly delimited by parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT

Mr. D'lEFEXBAKER:	I do not want to
get into an argument on that. The minister has mentioned the fact that the Labour party in Great Britain has passed an act extending the extraordinary powers for five years. In this parliament we are going to be asked to extend them for a period of one year, but I would point out that Britain put a control cm the exercise of the powers there by the provision that any order in council which is passed shall be laid on the table of parliament as soon as possible after it is passed, and that any member shall have the right to move to set aside an order in council so passed. While extraordinary powers are given, parliament retains control. That, I suggest, is the attitude which democratic assemblies should take.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT

Yes, but there is
a difference; and what is more, the government did not lay them all on the table. Some remained secret for a long time, and it was only when the press finally found out about their existence that they came to light. I am not, however, going to deal with that aspect of the matter except to say that laying them on the table does not give rights to individual members of parliament such as are guaranteed under the legislation in Great Britain, where any member of parliament may move and, if he secures the support of a sufficient number of members to that end, have the order in council cancelled, amended or abrogated. With sufficient, support he may move to cancel, amend or abrogate orders in council passed under these extraordinary powers.
I cannot understand why we should have any difference of opinion in this regard. All of us, I am sure, are desirous of returning as soon as possible to democratic principles and representative government now that the war is to all intents and purposes over, and I think these sections indicate a strange attitude on the part of the minister. Now that the war is over, he asks for powers which place him in a position of such absolute irresponsibility that he might subsidize one firm at the expense of another and in competition with a private company operating in the same area. I am sure the minister does not desire to obtain powers at the expense of parliament, and he should be willing to accept an amendment along that line.
There is one other matter, and that has to do with the various air fields.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT

speechtext:
It is wide enough to deal with almost anything. It provides that the governor in council may authorize the minister to enter into a contract with any corporation incorporated under section 20 of the act, for the organization, operation and maintenance of air services, and almost identical words are used in the United States aeronautical act. The maintenance of air services there has been defined as covering as well the operation of airports. I bring up this question of airports at this time because the opportunity may not come again for a considerable time. I am dealing now with the prairie provinces. I bring up with the minister the question of the establishment of the new T.C.A. line between Winnipeg, Saskatoon and Edmonton. I ask that assistance be given to the municipalities in connection with the development of their airfield facilities. Regardless of what part of western Canada we live in, all of us believe that some assistance should be given to assure that the Winnipeg airport shall be made adequate to handle the tremendous traffic that will find its way through that port. Anyone who travels by air realizes that the runways and flyways at each end need to be extended, and that a very great expansion should take place. I believe that representations along that line have been made to the minister from time to time.
This gives me the opportunity to ask him the following questions. I believe that several letters were sent to him by the St. James-Winnipeg airport commission. The last letter is dated October 5; the preceding one wras dated May 17 of this year. These letters were in regard to a plan prepared by the St. James-Winnipeg airport commission, which
189S
Trans-Canada Air Lines

was acceptable to the T.C.A., the municipality of St. James and the city of Winnipeg. I understand that representations were made to the minister and that he has not yet seen fit to reply to these letters; at least that is my information. Does he intend to accept the suggestions or recommendations of the St. James-Winnipeg airport commission, or has some other new plan been approved by the minister in reference to the expansion of airport facilities in Winnipeg? This organization which has been doing good work has been apparently endeavouring to interest the governments in the necessity of developing this airport and making it one of the great airports in the middle west. It has been in communication with the minister over a period of time. My information is that as yet he has not seen fit either to answer its suggestions or to put forth counter proposals. I would appreciate very much, and I know it' would, if he will make a statement generally in regard to the question of assisting municipalities in the prairie provinces and generally throughout the dominion with the development of their airports, and also in particular with respect to the recommendations and suggestions to which I have referred, which came from the St. James-Winnipeg airport commission.
There are great potentialities and possibilities in the development of aviation. All of us admit that one of our great difficulties in this country to-day stems from the fact that our airport facilities are not commensurate with the possibilities and potentialities of the situation. I suggest that the minister would be doing a worth-while work in reconstruction and in assuring employment and in the public works to which he has on occasion referred, to be undertaken in order to assist employment, if he assisted in the development of worth-while airports in this country. I suggest that he would be doing a great service if he undertook that work with a view to assisting in the assurance of employment and also in order to make available the best possible facilities for the post-war period. I offer these suggestions in a spirit of cooperation, desiring, as I know he desires, the greatest possible development for this country at this time.
One more thing which I would ask him to clarify is the matter of rates, the matter of charges, and the matter of transportation costs. In recent months substantial reductions have been made in passenger traffic rates in the United States. As a matter of fact, the reductions on the United States lines make it more attractive to travel by air to-day than by railroad. According to the evidence given (Mr. Diefenbaker.]
before the aeronautics committee in Washington, so far as ocean rates are concerned the reductions are such that in a very short time they will make travel by air less expensive than travel by ship, or certainly not very much greater. I ask the minister generally in regard to the present plans and the future plans of the T.C.A. to indicate to the committee and to the country some of his ideas with regard to transportation costs, the early possibility of reduction of passenger rates, and whether or not it is intended that in the operation of our extra-territorial lines, of our transoceanic lines, that the T.C.A. will be able to compete in rates against United States companies which are doing everything possible within their power to-day to monopolize ocean transportation.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
Our rates are reasonably competitive with those in the United States. They must be, because much of our business is competitive. We have a main line that runs parallel to the main lines of the United States. There is a difference, in that we allow discounts. We have a reduction for a return ticket, which I think is five per cent; we also have air travel cards which permit a reduction of fifteen per cent, but the net earnings from passengers per mile in Canada is only very slightly higher than the net earnings of competing lines in the United States. Reductions have been made from time to time in the rates charged passengers on Canadian lines. It may be necessary and perhaps desirable to do away with air travel cards and to make the rates exactly comparable with United States rates. Hon. members will appreciate that if we hope to take passengers from Toronto to Vancouver we must bear in mind that these passengers can travel through the Chicago gateway over a United States line to Seattle and thence to Vancouver; and if there is very much difference in the rates that is exactly

what they will do. maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
I am very glad that the
case of the M. & C. air line came up in this house to-night, because here is an example of what I have been trying to say for several years. That is, the feeder lines went out of business, not because they were bought up or taken over by this appallingly evil corporation known as the C.P.R., but because the volume of business that brought them into being dried up. In other words, the mines closed; prospecting ceased, and there was no business for the feeder air lines. In nearly every case that is why they have ceased to exist, not because

they have been bought up by somebody efse. They went out of existence because the business was not there; and the business was not there because we were in a deteriorating, declining cycle of mining. The M. and C. air service found that their business was gradually decreasing until they had use for only one plane which could not be profitably operated. Eventually, in order to be able to service the isolated mining community, this feeder company had to ask for and obtained a subsidy, and I think rightly so.
I should like to add one or two words about the proposed transpacific air line. There are several types of transoceanic air lines. There is the simple ferry type from here to Europe. That is intensely competitive, with rates carefully checked. In the near future we shall probably see the same arrangement with regard to air lines as the North Atlantic conference in connection with passenger shipping rates.
Then there is the somewhat longer but stilt highly competitive service to South America, a peculiarly attractive field for Canadian endeavour. Then there is the transpacific air line. It is quite probable that for many years this line, particularly the one to the orient. will not be a profitable venture. But it is a venture which in my opinion is most essential for the Canadian economy.
I wish to give one or two examples of what I mean. I represent an industrial riding. In that riding is a manufacturer of stoves. I understand that he does several times the amount of business outside Canada that he does inside Canada. His business outside Canada is in a large part with the orient. When the Sino-Japanese war occurred the result was a direct loss of employment in my constituency. When he was shipping to the orient he had the advantage of the assistance of the Canadian Pacific railway. Those people knew the orient; they knew the peculiarities of that market.
For instance, they found out-I mention this just to show the committee the intricacies of international trade-that a stove would not sell in China unless it had red handles and a red oven door. That may seem a simple thing to the committee, but to the Chinaman who was buying the stove it was very important. The Canadian Pacific agents and the people who knew the orient were able to point out to this stove manufacturer what he needed to do in order to sell his stoves.
I can give another example of the complexities of international trade. In China it is the practice to buy hot water from street vendors for the smallest Chinese coin, one cash. A great number of Chinese have the habit of buying one cash worth of hot water and

Trans-Canada Air Lines
putting this in a hot-water bottle to be carried in their belts in order to keep their stomachs warm in the cold weather. It is a simple and most practicable device. They had been able to buy only the larger hot-water bottles, but the people who were interested in developing trade suggested to a Canadian rubber manufacturer that he make a type of hot-water bottle that would hold just one cash worth of hot water. This was done, and a considerable amount of business developed providing additional employment and increased weekly payrolls.
This trade is known to the private companies. These companies are familiar with the oriental trade. If they have an interest in the air line they will also have an interest in shipping, because they go hand in glove.' While an air line carries passengers, many of them eventually become freight shippers. The result is that not only will your air line be profitable but your surface carrier will also be profitable if a large volume of business develops. If you divorce the private enterprise with its knowhow of trade in this peculiar market from your air service, are you likely to get the same efficiency as you would if the effectiveness of your service brought increased business in the orient to your surface carrier?
The success of the private company depends upon the success of the manufacturer in Canada. The private concern will do everything in their power to see that you get the service you need in the orient. If you are dealing with the government, the work of the govern-' ment concern will end with the effective transportation of the passenger. The knowledge which the Canadian Pacific has obtained of the oriental route should be utilized in setting up our Canadian transpacific route.
I am satisfied that at the moment no air line across, the Pacific will be profitable, but we should look farther than that. This matter stretches into the very heart of industrial Canada. Which is likely to be the best for the country, the organization which will help you find markets in order that revenues may be created for its surface carrier, or the gov-, emment concern, whose responsibility ends with your safe deliveiy at the airport in the orient? That is the basic difference between a privately operated air line across the Pacific and a government-operated air line.
In the pre-war years we in Canada were,' and I think justly so, proud of having one of the largest transpacific services. It was certainly the fastest, and 'as far as freight goes I think it was even larger than the N.Y.K., the government-owned Japanese line. We are peculiarly interested in the orient which offers a tremendous market for Canadian goods. If we are to develop that market we must use every bit of information upon which we can get our hands. We shall be faced with bitter competition for that market. The Canadian Pacific has the know-how, and I suggest that it is folly to exclude that company from any participation in transpacific air service.

The hon. member for Vancouver East said a while ago that I had made the statement that under government ownership there would be fewer jobs than under private ownership, or that was the gist of what he said. I should like to read from the evidence of the standing committee on railways and shipping, at page 203, where Mr. Symington said this in regard to the $25,000,000, which is what we are now considering. He said:
* When you come to the international, of course you need-why $25,000,000 is nothing, nothing at all, in this game. There is not an air line in the United States which has not increased" its capital spending by at least $100,000,000, not $25,009,000. If you could see the money that is being expended in this international game, it would give you pause. It gives me pause. Certainly I am not going to spend money the way those fellows have been spending it. When you look at their balance sheet, I am not in the same class with them.
The reason I bring that point out in answer to the statement of the hon. member for
Trans-Canada Air Lines

Vancouver East is that this is an example quoted by Mr. Symington of what is being done in the United States where private enterprise is allowed to flourish and provide service to the people and create opportunities for young Americans in contrast with what is envisaged under this bill, where $25,000,000 is asked for as compared with the 8100,000,000 asked for by any one of a number of United States companies.

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: Will the hon. member answer one question? I have listened for hours to him, and I should like to know if he is in favour of expanding the service,, on Trans-Canada Air Lines or if he is opposed. Will he answer yes or no?

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: I am in favour of providing service and opportunity to the Canadian people, and I believe that the proper .and best way of doing it is through private enterprise.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 2-Power to issue securities.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: Will the minister explain what procedure will be followed after there has been a divesting order?

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: There is nothing in this bill which has anything to do with the divesting order. There is nothing here to provide any money, to cover the divesting order. I cannot tell my hon. friend what I am going to do.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: I am being polite and the minister had better keep his temper with me. I am not asking provocative questions. I asked a perfectly proper question.

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: Would my hon. friend give me the reference to the divesting order?

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: If the minister will sit down and let me put my question he will have no reason for becoming so fussed up. This section provides that the Canadian National Railways shall at some time take up this new capital. We are told that in due course there will be a divesting order, and I am asking the minister what will happen in that event. In the first place, if the shares have already beeft taken up by the C.N.R., or, in the second place, if they have not been taken up by the C.N.R. at that time, what procedure will be followed in either case? Will the shares then be held by the minister personally as trustee for the crown?

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
While I might say that no plans have so far been made and that the government's policy will be announced in due course, the fact of the matter is that there is a clause in the contract between the govern-

ment and the Canadian National Railways which permits the government to recapture the shares of the company whenever it wishes. It is in the Trans-Canada bill that the government has the right to take over the shares.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 3-Authorization to deal with shares of companies incorporated under section 20.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: This section is one of those about which there was some question with regard to its being used for operations beyond the boundaries of Canada. The minister has said repeatedly to-day and during the sittings of the committee on railways and shipping that there was no intention of acquiring the shares of domestic companies. I submit to him once more, that being the announced government policy, the bill itself should go no farther. Yet the minister said to-night that the bill does go farther and does give Trans-Canada Air Lines power to acquire shares in a company flying in Canada only. Would he have any objection to an amendment to that section by adding the words "outside of Canada" which would give Trans-Canada Air Lines full power to acquire shares in a company operating outside of Canada but would not give them power to acquire shares in a company operating solely within Canada? Then, if at a later date it was the wish of the government to change that policy and * acquire shares of a company flying within Canada, an amendment could be brought in. But I suggest to him that it would be fair only to go so far now in the bill as government policy itself goes, and yet the bill admittedly goes farther.

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: Would my hon. friend explain his reasoning and show how the public interest would be greatly protected by such a step and the well-being of the Canadian people be served thereby? I should like to have a reason for doing it.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: The difficulty is this. When you put a provision of this type in a bill it_ leaves a sword hanging over the heads of people who are trying to develop air lines. That, I think, is unwise because it may prevent them from making the expansions which they otherwise would make. The bill should only go so far as government policy itself goes.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: And what about those veterans of whom the minister spoke?

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
There is nothing in the section that holds a sword over the head of anyone

Trans-Canada Air Lines
or that could hold a sword over anyone. That theory is entirely without foundation. I think the section should stand without amendment.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
I move, Mr. Chairman, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver South, that the words "outside of Canada" be added to section 3 (e) after the words "any kind" in line 27 of the bill.
Amendment negatived.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: I should like to ask the ministfer whether, under paragraph (f), there will be any limit on the amount of money which can be lent.. Surely there should be some limit in a case like this.

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
The amount will be limited
to what the operation requires and Trans-Canada Air Lines have at their disposal for the purpose, and subject to the approval of this parliament and of the committee on railways and shipping, which must approve the investment.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 4-Limitation of power, to sell or dispose of shares of companies incorporated under section 20.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: As to flying over certain countries of South America, Brazil, I know7, and Venezuela, I think, demand that a passenger air line must give to the flown-over country a certain percentage of the stock of the company. Can the minister tell us what these percentages are, because we may be flying over a number of countries and that might eat up a considerable percentage of the capital.

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: There are regulations, differing in every country. They are not such as would prevent Trans-Canada Air Lines from operating into Brazil if it cares to do so. I cannot give the requirements of each country, and I think that matter could be left to a future parliament. No immediate operation is intended.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
Section 5 agreed to.
On section 6-Contract provisions.

speechtext:

here makes it possible for the Trans-Canada contract to be worded pursuant to order in council, rather than as set out in the original act. It has been my understanding that under this section of the act routes which are to be flown by Trans-Canada have first been designated as such, and that designation is made by order in council. It is not clear from the
bill whether that policy is to be continued. In other words, will government policy be in the future that all routes to be flown by Trans-Canada Air Lines will be designated by order in council, as has been the case in the past?

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT

Yes. These contracts are
made through ou>r own post office as a rule, but we have the power to make contracts with the post office of any country.

speechtext:
They are made through
the post office of the flown-over country?

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
The Canadian post office, as
a rule.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT

They are made between the
air lines and the post office.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: And the post office of the foreign country?
